newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Fears of huge flood costs hit Czech capital mkts.
newsitem.headline: Fears of huge flood costs hit Czech capital mkts.

text.p: The Czech crown, along with stocks and bonds, fell on Monday as a wave of fear over the economic costs of heavy flooding in the Czech Republic broke over the country's capital markets.

As the death toll in the worst flooding in the region in a century reached 37, analysts raced to tally the cost of the damage caused by the flood wave which has put nearly a third of the country under water.

Analysts said investor sentiment, weak to begin with, has fallen even further given estimates damage may total as much as 100 billion crowns ($2.93 billion), and could cost the already sluggish economy up to one full percentage point in GDP growth this year.

"Both direct damage and economic losses are estimated at tens of billions of crowns (and) by comparison, one percent of projected GDP for this year is 16.5 billion crowns," said Jiri Krovak, chief economist at WoodCommerz.
"Thus, the flood (damage) is in percentage points of GDP, not fractions," he added.
The Czech crown fell early on Monday, breaking through its support level of 19 to the mark before steadying at around the central bank's daily fixing of 19.04.
Analysts said concerns over possible effects of the flood, including larger budget and trade deficits, coupled with an easing of demand for crowns could push the currency even lower.

"There has been another wave of foreign currency buying this morning and for the time being it seems that the interest to go short in the Czech crown is over," said Breta Tichanek of ING bank in Prague.
Added Matt Starr of Creditanstalt in Prague: "These factors point to a weaker currency as slower growth and greater imports will push higher the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP."

The floods covering low-lying areas of the eastern third of the Czech Republic -- as well as parts of Poland, Austria and Slovakia -- have forced tens of thousands from their homes, and closed several major industrial concerns.
Among the larger firms affected are tyre maker Barum Continental and Skoda Automobilova, both of which are major exporters.

Analysts said it may take three months for some firms to be back up and running at full capacity, biting hard into their bottom lines and giving already finicky investors yet another reason to avoid Czech equities.

"There are still no firm estimates of the flood damage, but I think the market feels the costs will be quite high. Given this, some construction and materials issues may benefit, but the overall outlook is a little pessimistic," a foreign trader said.

The Prague Stock Exchange, mired in a slump almost since the beginning of the year, has fallen even quicker since the flooding began, losing 0.3 percent at its daily fixing, and nearly three percent over the past week.
Starr said bonds have also failed to escape the calamity, and just as they were rebounding from historic lows following a crisis in the crown currency at the end of May.

He said that as the crown began to look weak, speculators moved quickly to borrow at cheap levels, pushing the six month Prague Interbank Offered Rate (PRIBOR) up about four perecentage points to around 18-19 percent.
"(This) in turn caused panic selling of both corporate and government bonds," Starr said.
Analysts added that parliament's approval on Friday to issue up to five billion crowns worth of bonds to raise funds for disaster relief may flood the market with paper, and hurt prices even further.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
($ = 34.11 Czech Crowns)
